title: opcua: add decryption support
description:
This MR adds support for decrypting OPC UA traffic.
The server or client logs the ephemeral AES encryption keys and IVs and Wireshark loads this file (similar to TLS).
The correct keys are found by comparing OPC UA SecureChannelId and TokenId.

Supported Security Profiles: All with either AES128-CBC or AES256-CBC as symmetric encryption algorithm.
* Basic128Rsa15
* Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep
* Basic256Sha256
* Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss

Limitations:

* OpenSecureChannel Request/Response cannot be decrypted, because these are RSA encrypted.
* The newer ChaCha20-Poly1305 is not supported yet, only AES.

Pros:

* The symmetric decryption does not require the RSA private keys. The concept will work also with ECC based policies and ECDH key exchange.

This causes a large number of dissector bug messages on the `opcua-signed.pcapng` file when opened in Wireshark. I believe that is because the dissector is storing the state of whether or not signing (and encryption) is being used in the conversation data; that state is accurate for the next frame when doing sequential processing, but with random order dissection, as in a second pass in tshark or when clicking on a different packet in Wireshark, the state sometimes has the wrong value.

I believe it works properly in single-pass tshark. A number of dissectors have had this same issue before; when dissection has state, a packet being dissected on the second or later passed needs to know the state at the time that the same packet was dissected on the first pass.

For example, if you open `opcua-signed.pcapng` in Wireshark and click on packet 8 or 9 (which are encrypted) and then packets 4 or 6, there is no error, but if you click on one of packets 10-16 and then click on packet 4 or 6, then there is a dissector bug message because it is trying to dissect a signature that isn't on the Hello or Acknowledge packet.
AFAICS the problem was caused by parsing the service payload for service types that have no payload. I fixed this issue in !12832

+#ifndef __OPCUA_KEYSET_H__
+#define __OPCUA_KEYSET_H__
+
+#include <stdint.h>
+
+/** symmetric encryption keyset */
+struct ua_keyset {
+    uint64_t id; /** keyset identifier: combination of securechannel_id and token_id */
+    unsigned char client_iv[16]; /**< Client side IV. Always 128 bit. */
+    unsigned char server_iv[16]; /**< Server side IV. Always 128 bit. */
+    unsigned char client_key[32]; /**< client encryption key */
+    unsigned char server_key[32]; /**< server encryption key */
+    unsigned int client_key_len; /**< AES key length: 16 (AES-128) or 32 (AES-256) */
+    unsigned int server_key_len; /**< AES key length: 16 (AES-128) or 32 (AES-256) */
+    unsigned int client_sig_len; /**< Client side symmetric signture length. */
+    unsigned int server_sig_len; /**< Server side symmetric signture length. */
+};
+
+int ua_keysets_init(void);
+int ua_keysets_clear(void);
+
+/**
+ * Creates a unique keyset id from securechannel_id and token_id.
+ *
+ * @param securechannel_id Identifies the secure channel to be able to distinguish
+ *   different connections. This is a randomly generated id.
+ * @param token_id Identifies the keyset of a channel. This number normally starts with
+ *   1 and gets incremented with every secure channel renew.
+ *
+ * @return 64bit Id.
+ */
+static inline uint64_t ua_keyset_id(uint32_t securechannel_id, uint32_t token_id)
+{
+    return ((uint64_t)securechannel_id << 32) | token_id;
+}
+
+struct ua_keyset *ua_keysets_add(void);
+void ua_keysets_sort(void);
+struct ua_keyset *ua_keysets_lookup(uint64_t id);
+void ua_keysets_dump(void);
+
+#endif /* __OPCUA_KEYSET_H__ */
